query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small, trace amount of Hf (around 0.5 atomic %) to the eutectic high-entropy alloy will improve both the room-temperature tensile strength and ductility by promoting the formation of Hf‐rich precipitates at the lamellar colony internal boundaries, thereby reinforcing these interfaces and inhibiting microcrack initiation and propagation.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries that serve as microcrack nucleation sites during room-temperature tensile deformation
generation.intervention: Introduce a trace Hf addition (≈0.5 atomic %) into the alloy composition during processing
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation conditions with standard thermo-mechanical processing routes for eutectic HEAs
generation.structural_mediator: Hf-rich precipitates localized at phase and grain boundaries within the lamellar colonies
generation.mechanism: The trace Hf is expected to form fine intermetallic precipitates at the colony boundaries, which strengthen the interfaces (via interface pinning) and impede the nucleation and propagation of microcracks while also contributing to precipitation strengthening of the harder phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified baseline alloy, the Hf-modified alloy will exhibit a higher yield strength and an increased tensile ductility (i.e. greater strain before failure), due to the dual benefits of reinforced colony boundaries and additional precipitation strengthening.
generation.baseline: The conventional eutectic HEA with lamellar microstructure processed without trace Hf addition, which typically shows a trade-off between strength and ductility due to microcrack initiation at internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective in eutectic HEAs where well-defined lamellar colonies exist; its applicability may be limited in alloys without such a dual-phase microstructure or where the Hf concentration alters the primary phases substantially.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimum Hf concentration and the detailed nature of the Hf-rich precipitate formation under room-temperature tensile loading remain to be fully quantified; effects may also depend on subtle variations in processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set with the standard eutectic HEA composition and the other with an additional trace (~0.5 at.%) of Hf. Process both sets under identical conditions. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests to compare yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility. Complement tensile testing with microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM) to identify and compare the presence and distribution of Hf-rich precipitates at the colony boundaries.
measurements: Microstructure analysis (precipitate size, distribution, and location at internal boundaries)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in both yield strength and ductility compared to the baseline, or if microstructural characterization fails to show the formation of Hf-rich precipitates at the colony boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As we all know, the alloying of metals with certain specific elements can very effectively improve alloy properties through various strengthening methods such as precipitation strengthening, solution strengthening, and interface strengthening [,,,]. Hf is an essential alloying element for both the interface strengthening of superalloys and the strengthening of the Ni-Al B2 phase [,,,,,]. Recently, some studies have shown that adding a small amount of Hf to a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy could improve the room-temperature mechanical property of the alloy without significantly reducing the ductility of the alloy through the precipitation of intermetallic compounds such as Ni7Hf2 and Laves phases [,]. However, these studies mainly focus on single-phase high-entropy alloys, and the addition of Hf is relatively large, usually more than one atom. Therefore, the effect of trace Hf addition on the properties of the alloy at room temperature and high temperature is worthy of in-depth investigation.

The strengthening effect of Hf on the alloy could be maintained at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C.At different high temperatures, the Hf0.5 alloy exhibited a higher strength and ductility than the Hf0 alloys. The outstanding high-temperature strength of the Hf0.5 alloy was attributed to the precipitation strengthening of the Hf-rich phase precipitated in the inner of the B2 phase. The excellent high-temperature ductility of the Hf0.5 alloy was attributed to the pinning effect of the Hf-rich phase that existed at grain and phase boundaries to boundary sliding during the high-temperature deformation.
